items.title: Causes of the Revolt of 1857
items.body:
## In one line

The Revolt of 1857 was the first big, armed challenge to British rule, and it happened because anger had been building up for years among princes, soldiers, peasants and ordinary people all at once.

## The story

Think of the causes as pressure building in a sealed pot, with the greased cartridge as the lid finally blowing off.

Over the previous decades, British policies had hurt almost everyone. Craftsmen lost their livelihood because cheap machine-made British cloth flooded India while Indian cloth faced heavy taxes in Britain. Peasants were squeezed by high land taxes. Indian kings and landlords lost their thrones and estates through British takeover policies. Soldiers (sepoys) were paid less than British troops, were ordered to serve across the sea against their caste beliefs, and felt their religion was under attack. On top of all this came a rumour in 1857 that the new rifle cartridges were greased with cow fat and pig fat — the single spark that lit the fire.

Historians usually sort these grievances into five groups.

| Group | What made people angry |
|---|---|
| **Economic** | Loss of handicrafts (de-industrialisation); tariffs above 80% on Indian textiles in Britain while British goods entered India tax-free; heavy land revenue; farmers pushed from food crops to cash crops |
| **Political** | Subsidiary Alliance, the **Doctrine of Lapse** (under Dalhousie) and outright annexation — most of all **Awadh in 1856** — which stripped Indian rulers of power and dignity |
| **Administrative** | Corruption in police and courts; Indians kept out of higher posts; loss of royal patronage for artists and scholars |
| **Socio-religious** | The **Religious Disabilities Act, 1850** (let converts to Christianity inherit property); reforms like banning Sati (1829) and the Widow Remarriage Act (1856) felt intrusive; fear of forced conversion; racial insults |
| **Military** | The **General Service Enlistment Act, 1856** forcing overseas service against caste rules; lower pay and poorer treatment of Indian sepoys |

## Why it matters / why it is asked

Almost every prelims paper tests one of these causes, and the examiner's favourite trick is to misplace an example in the wrong group (for example, calling the Doctrine of Lapse a military cause). Mains uses the same five heads as the skeleton of a full essay answer.

## Picture it

```
Slow build-up (years) ............... Spark (1857)
Economic + Political + Admin  --->  Greased Enfield
+ Socio-religious + Military         cartridge rumour
            = REVOLT
```

## Terms explained

- **Doctrine of Lapse** — a British rule that if an Indian king died with no natural son, his kingdom was taken over by the British (an adopted son was not allowed to inherit).
- **Subsidiary Alliance** — a deal where an Indian ruler kept British troops, paid for them, and gave up his independent foreign policy.
- **Sepoy** — an Indian soldier serving in the British (East India Company) army.
- **De-industrialisation** — the decline of India's traditional handloom and craft industries under colonial trade policy.
- **Religious Disabilities Act, 1850** — also called the Caste Disabilities Removal Act; it let a person who changed religion still inherit family property, which Hindus saw as encouraging conversion.

## Don't confuse

- The **greased cartridge** was the *immediate* cause (the spark), not a deep cause. If a question asks for the "immediate cause", the answer is the cartridge, not the Doctrine of Lapse.
- **Doctrine of Lapse** (annexation if no natural heir) is different from the **Subsidiary Alliance** (keeping paid British troops).

## Remember it

Hook: **"PEAMS"** = **P**olitical, **E**conomic, **A**dministrative, **M**ilitary, **S**ocio-religious — the five groups of causes. Spark on top = greased cartridge.

## TL;DR

- Five groups of causes: economic, political, administrative, socio-religious, military.
- Political = Subsidiary Alliance + Doctrine of Lapse + annexation of Awadh (1856).
- Socio-religious = Religious Disabilities Act 1850 + resented reforms (Sati ban, Widow Remarriage Act 1856).
- Military = General Service Enlistment Act 1856 (overseas service) + unequal pay.
- Immediate spark = greased Enfield cartridges (cow fat offended Hindus, pig fat offended Muslims).
keyPoints: Five heads of causes: economic, political, administrative, socio-religious and military.
Political cause = Subsidiary Alliance, Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie) and annexations such as Awadh (1856).
Socio-religious = Religious Disabilities Act 1850 plus resented reforms (Sati abolition, Widow Remarriage Act 1856).
Military = General Service Enlistment Act 1856 requiring overseas service, plus unequal pay.
Immediate cause = greased Enfield cartridges offending Hindus (cow fat) and Muslims (pig fat).

items.title: Outbreak & Course of the Revolt
items.body:
## In one line

This note traces how the revolt actually began — from one soldier's protest at Barrackpore, to the full mutiny at Meerut, to the march on Delhi where a Mughal emperor became its figurehead.

## The story

The trouble started inside the army. **Mangal Pandey**, a soldier of the 34th Native Infantry, attacked his British officers at **Barrackpore** (near Calcutta) on **29 March 1857**; he was tried and **hanged on 8 April 1857**. This was the first flashpoint.

The real explosion came at **Meerut**. There, **85 sepoys** refused to use the new cartridges, so the British court-martialled and jailed them on 9 May. The next day, **10 May 1857**, their comrades rose in open rebellion, freed them, and killed British officers. These Meerut soldiers then marched straight to **Delhi** and declared the old Mughal emperor **Bahadur Shah Zafar (II)** the leader of the revolt — this gave the uprising a single symbol that rulers and rebels across the north could rally behind.

From Delhi the revolt spread widely. It was not just soldiers: **peasants, artisans, shopkeepers and zamindars** joined in, attacking law courts and revenue (tax) offices because these were the everyday face of British power.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

Dates and the sequence (Barrackpore → Meerut → Delhi) are classic prelims matching material. The civilian participation is the key evidence Mains answers use to argue the revolt was "more than a mutiny".

## Picture it

```
29 Mar 1857   Barrackpore  - Mangal Pandey attacks officers (hanged 8 Apr)
 9 May 1857   Meerut       - 85 sepoys jailed for refusing cartridges
10 May 1857   Meerut       - open revolt breaks out
   then  -->  Delhi        - Bahadur Shah Zafar proclaimed leader
```

## Terms explained

- **Native Infantry** — a regiment of Indian foot soldiers in the Company army; the "34th" was its number.
- **Court-martial** — a military trial of a soldier.
- **Zamindar** — a landholder who collected rent/revenue from peasants.
- **Revenue office** — the government office that collected land tax; a symbol of British control.

## Don't confuse

- **Mangal Pandey (Barrackpore, 29 March)** came *before* the main outbreak; the general revolt began at **Meerut on 10 May 1857**. Do not mix the two dates.
- Bahadur Shah Zafar was the *symbolic* head; the actual fighting commander at Delhi was **Bakht Khan**.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Barrackpore sparks, Meerut burns, Delhi crowns"** — spark (Mangal Pandey), fire (Meerut 10 May), figurehead (Bahadur Shah Zafar).

## TL;DR

- Mangal Pandey attacked officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 (hanged 8 April 1857).
- 85 sepoys jailed at Meerut on 9 May; open revolt on 10 May 1857.
- Meerut sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar the leader.
- Spread from Punjab to the Narmada and from Bihar to Rajputana.
- Peasants, artisans, shopkeepers and zamindars joined, attacking courts and revenue offices.

items.title: Major Centres, Leaders & British Commanders
items.body:
## In one line

This note is a memory map: which city rose in revolt, who led it, and which British officer crushed it.

## The story

The revolt had no single battlefield. Instead, several cities rose at once, each under a local leader. Delhi had the emperor and his general; Kanpur had Nana Sahib; Lucknow had a queen fighting for her young son; Jhansi had the famous Rani Lakshmi Bai. Because the centres acted separately, the British could pick them off one by one — which is also a big reason the revolt failed.

Against these leaders the British sent a set of commanders, each remembered for a particular city or victory. Learning the two tables together — rebel leaders and British commanders — is the fastest way to answer the matching questions.

### Rebel centres and their leaders

| Centre | Rebel leader(s) |
|---|---|
| Delhi | Bahadur Shah Zafar, General **Bakht Khan** |
| Kanpur | **Nana Sahib**, Tatya Tope |
| Lucknow | **Begum Hazrat Mahal**, Birjis Qadir |
| Jhansi | **Rani Lakshmi Bai** |
| Bareilly | Khan Bahadur Khan |
| Faizabad | Maulvi Ahmadullah |
| Arrah (Bihar) | **Kunwar Singh**, Amar Singh |
| Baghpat | Shah Mal |

### British commanders who suppressed it

| Official | Role |
|---|---|
| Sir Colin Campbell | Commander-in-Chief; suppressed the revolt, relieved Lucknow |
| Sir Hugh Rose | Defeated Rani Lakshmi Bai |
| Henry Havelock | Key role in recapturing Kanpur |
| Colonel James Neill | Suppressed the revolt at Banaras |

## Why it matters / why it is asked

Match-the-following between centres, leaders and British officers is one of the most repeated question types in both APPSC and UPSC prelims. One wrong pairing loses the mark.

## Picture it

```
Delhi    -> Bahadur Shah Zafar / Bakht Khan
Kanpur   -> Nana Sahib / Tatya Tope
Lucknow  -> Begum Hazrat Mahal / Birjis Qadir
Jhansi   -> Rani Lakshmi Bai     (crushed by Hugh Rose)
Arrah    -> Kunwar Singh
```

## Terms explained

- **Begum** — a Muslim lady of high rank; Begum Hazrat Mahal fought on behalf of her son Birjis Qadir.
- **Maulvi** — a Muslim religious scholar; Maulvi Ahmadullah led the Faizabad rebels.
- **Commander-in-Chief** — the top military officer of the whole army (here, Sir Colin Campbell).
- **Relieved Lucknow** — broke the rebel siege and rescued the trapped British garrison there.

## Don't confuse

- **Nana Sahib (Kanpur)** vs **Rani Lakshmi Bai (Jhansi)** — a common swap in matching questions.
- **Begum Hazrat Mahal** led **Lucknow**, not Kanpur.
- **Hugh Rose** defeated the Rani of Jhansi; **Colin Campbell** was the overall Commander-in-Chief — don't interchange them.

## Remember it

Hook: **"King in Delhi, Nana in Kanpur, Begum in Lucknow, Rani in Jhansi, Kunwar in Arrah."** For the British side: **"Campbell commands, Rose beats the Rani."**

## TL;DR

- Delhi — Bahadur Shah Zafar & Bakht Khan; Kanpur — Nana Sahib & Tatya Tope.
- Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal & Birjis Qadir; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmi Bai.
- Bareilly — Khan Bahadur Khan; Faizabad — Maulvi Ahmadullah; Arrah — Kunwar Singh.
- Sir Colin Campbell (C-in-C) and Sir Hugh Rose (defeated Rani Lakshmi Bai) led the suppression.
- Henry Havelock recaptured Kanpur; James Neill suppressed Banaras.
keyPoints: Delhi — Bahadur Shah Zafar & Bakht Khan; Kanpur — Nana Sahib & Tatya Tope.
Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal & Birjis Qadir; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmi Bai.
Bareilly — Khan Bahadur Khan; Faizabad — Maulvi Ahmadullah; Arrah — Kunwar Singh.
Sir Colin Campbell (C-in-C) and Sir Hugh Rose (defeated Rani Lakshmi Bai) led the suppression.
Henry Havelock recaptured Kanpur; James Neill suppressed Banaras.

items.title: Suppression & Reasons for Failure
items.body:
## In one line

This note explains how the British crushed the revolt by late 1857–59, and the clear reasons why the rebels, despite their numbers, lost.

## The story

The British struck back hard. They **recaptured Delhi on 20 September 1857**, took the old emperor **Bahadur Shah Zafar** prisoner and **exiled him to Rangoon** (in Burma), executing his sons. **Rani Lakshmi Bai** died fighting; **Tatya Tope** was captured and **executed in 1859**. The suppression was brutal — about **150,000 Indians**, including many civilians, were killed.

Why did a revolt with so many fighters fail? Five reasons stand out. It stayed penned into the north (the south and most of the east and west, including Andhra, stayed quiet). The leaders never united under one plan or one goal. The British simply had better weapons and, crucially, the **telegraph** to move news and troops faster than the rebels. Several powerful Indian princes actively helped the British. And many landlords and educated Indians kept their distance, seeing the revolt as a step backwards.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

The "reasons for failure" is a guaranteed Mains sub-question and a frequent statement-based prelims item (the telegraph and loyal princely states are favourite options). The exile of Bahadur Shah Zafar and the execution of Tatya Tope (1859) are common date/fact questions.

## Picture it

| Why it failed | One-line reason |
|---|---|
| Limited spread | Mainly North India; south/east/west mostly calm |
| No unity | Local leaders, no common plan or ideology |
| British edge | Better arms + the telegraph |
| Loyal princes | Gwalior, Indore, Hyderabad, Sikh rulers helped Britain |
| Social split | Many zamindars and educated Indians stayed aloof |

## Terms explained

- **Exiled to Rangoon** — sent away as a prisoner to Rangoon (now Yangon, Myanmar), never allowed to return.
- **Telegraph** — the then-new electric system for sending messages instantly over wires; it let the British coordinate faster than the rebels.
- **Loyal (princely) states** — Indian kingdoms that chose to support the British instead of the rebels.
- **Aloof** — staying away and not taking part.

## Don't confuse

- The telegraph helped the **British**, not the rebels — a classic "odd statement out" trap.
- **Tatya Tope** was executed in **1859** (after the main revolt), not during 1857.

## Remember it

Hook: **"No map, no leader, no wires, no friends"** — limited spread, no unity, no technology, no princely support. That is why 1857 failed.

## TL;DR

- Delhi recaptured on 20 September 1857; Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled to Rangoon.
- Rani Lakshmi Bai killed in battle; Tatya Tope executed in 1859; ~150,000 Indians killed.
- Failure factors: limited spread, no unified leadership, superior British arms and telegraph.
- Loyal states — Gwalior (Scindia), Indore (Holkar), Hyderabad (Nizam) and Sikh rulers helped the British.
- Class divisions — many zamindars and educated Indians stayed aloof.
keyPoints: Delhi recaptured on 20 September 1857; Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled to Rangoon.
Rani Lakshmi Bai killed in battle; Tatya Tope executed in 1859; ~150,000 Indians killed.
Failure factors: limited spread, no unified leadership, superior British arms and telegraph.
Loyal states — Gwalior (Scindia), Indore (Holkar), Hyderabad (Nizam) and Sikh rulers helped the British.
Class divisions — many zamindars and educated Indians stayed aloof.

items.title: Consequences — Act of 1858, Proclamation & Army Reform
items.body:
## In one line

The revolt failed, but it changed everything: it ended the East India Company's rule and handed India directly to the British Crown, with a new promise to the people and a reorganised army.

## The story

The British realised that letting a trading company govern India was no longer safe. So the **Government of India Act, 1858** took India away from the **East India Company** and placed it under the **British Crown** (the Queen). A new minister in London, the **Secretary of State for India** — a member of the British Cabinet, answerable to Parliament and helped by a **Council of 15** — now ran Indian affairs. The old Governor-General got an extra title, **Viceroy**, meaning the Queen's personal representative; **Lord Canning** was the first Viceroy.

To calm the people, the Queen issued the **Queen's Proclamation of 1858**. It promised not to interfere in religion, to give Indians equal chance in government jobs (a promise mostly ignored in practice), and to stop seizing princely states.

Finally, the British fixed the army that had rebelled. On the advice of the **Peel Commission**, they put more British soldiers in proportion to Indians, mixed up units by caste, community and region so soldiers could not easily unite again, kept Indians out of the artillery (the big guns), and recruited more Sikhs and Gurkhas.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

The 1858 Act and the Queen's Proclamation are the single most tested "consequence" facts. Prelims loves three-statement questions mixing the Secretary of State, the Viceroy title and the end of Company rule. The Peel Commission's "divide the army" logic is a favourite too.

## Picture it

```
Before 1858:  East India Company governs India
     | Revolt of 1857
     v
After 1858:   British Crown governs India
   - Secretary of State for India (London, in Cabinet)
   - Governor-General = also Viceroy (Canning, first)
   - Queen's Proclamation: no religious interference, no more annexation
   - Peel Commission: more British troops, mixed units, no Indian artillery
```

## Terms explained

- **The Crown** — the British monarch (Queen Victoria); "Crown rule" means direct rule by the British government instead of the Company.
- **Secretary of State for India** — the British Cabinet minister in London responsible for India.
- **Viceroy** — the title of the Governor-General as the Queen's personal representative in India.
- **Peel Commission** — the committee that recommended how to re-organise the Indian army after 1857.
- **Artillery** — the heavy guns and cannon units of an army.

## Don't confuse

- The **Secretary of State for India** sat in **London** (in the Cabinet); the **Viceroy** sat in India. They are different offices.
- The Proclamation *promised* equal job opportunity, but this was **not actually implemented** — a common "was it kept?" trap.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Company out, Crown in; Canning becomes Viceroy; divide the army."**

## TL;DR

- GoI Act 1858 ended Company rule, transferring India to the British Crown.
- Created the Secretary of State for India (Cabinet member, aided by a Council); Canning = first Viceroy.
- Queen's Proclamation 1858 promised non-interference in religion and an end to annexations.
- Peel Commission raised the British:Indian troop ratio, segregated units and barred Indians from artillery.
- Aftermath: rise of nationalism, 'divide and rule', and 'masterly inactivity' abroad.
keyPoints: GoI Act 1858 ended Company rule, transferring India to the British Crown.
Created the Secretary of State for India (Cabinet member, aided by a Council); Canning = first Viceroy.
Queen's Proclamation 1858 promised non-interference in religion and an end to annexations.
Peel Commission raised the British:Indian troop ratio, segregated units and barred Indians from artillery.
Aftermath: rise of nationalism, 'divide and rule', and 'masterly inactivity' abroad.

items.title: Administrative Structure After 1857
items.body:
## In one line

After 1857 the British slowly built a new governing machine — a law-making council with a few nominated Indians, a province system, and a gradual sharing of money between the centre and the provinces.

## The story

Having taken direct control, the Crown needed a working administration. The **Indian Councils Act of 1861** added an **Imperial Legislative Council** to help the Governor-General make laws. The Governor-General could nominate **6 to 12 extra members**, at least half of them **non-official** (Indians or Englishmen outside government) — usually princes, big landlords, merchants or retired officers. But this council had almost no real power: it could not touch the budget, could not question the government, and any law needed the Governor-General's approval and could even be cancelled by the Secretary of State in London.

For day-to-day rule, India was split into **provinces**. The three oldest, the **Presidencies of Bengal, Madras and Bombay**, had Governors with more powers; the rest were run by Lieutenant Governors or Chief Commissioners.

Money was the next problem. Running everything from the centre was clumsy, so three Viceroys gradually handed financial responsibility to the provinces, as the table shows.

| Viceroy | Reform |
|---|---|
| **Lord Mayo (1870)** | First separated central and provincial finances by giving provinces **fixed grants** for police, jails, education, roads |
| **Lord Lytton (1877)** | Transferred more items — **land revenue, excise, general administration, law & justice** |
| **Lord Ripon (1882)** | Divided revenues into **general, provincial and shared**, reviewed every **five years** |

## Why it matters / why it is asked

The 1861 Act is the start of "Indians in law-making" and is heavily tested (nominated vs elected is the trap). The Mayo–Lytton–Ripon finance sequence is a classic match-the-Viceroy question.

## Picture it

```
1861  Imperial Legislative Council (nominated members, advice only)
1870  Mayo    -> fixed grants to provinces
1877  Lytton  -> more heads handed over (land revenue, excise...)
1882  Ripon   -> general + provincial + shared revenues (5-yearly)
```

## Terms explained

- **Imperial Legislative Council** — the central body that advised the Governor-General on making laws.
- **Non-official member** — a member who was not a serving government officer (could be an Indian prince, landlord or merchant).
- **Nominated** — chosen/appointed by the Governor-General (not elected by the people).
- **Presidency** — one of the three major administrative units (Bengal, Madras, Bombay) headed by a Governor.
- **Excise** — a tax on goods produced inside the country (for example, on liquor or salt).

## Don't confuse

- Members of the 1861 Council were **nominated, not elected** — the most common trap in this topic.
- Financial **decentralisation** (sharing money with provinces) is different from political power — the Council still had **no budgetary power**.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Mayo gives, Lytton gives more, Ripon shares"** (1870 → 1877 → 1882) for the finance sequence.

## TL;DR

- Indian Councils Act 1861 created the Imperial Legislative Council for law-making.
- Members were nominated (6-12, half non-official); the Council was purely consultative with no budgetary power.
- A bill needed the Governor-General's assent and could be disallowed by the Secretary of State.
- Financial decentralization: Mayo (1870) fixed grants; Lytton (1877) more heads; Ripon (1882) shared revenues.
- Three Presidencies (Bengal, Madras, Bombay) had more powers than other provinces.

items.title: Tribal, Peasant & Civil Uprisings (before & after 1857)
items.body:
## In one line

Besides the big revolt of 1857, many smaller tribal and peasant uprisings fought the British — and the exam loves to pair their names, leaders and special terms (like 'Ulgulan') with 1857.

## The story

British rule did not only anger soldiers and princes. In the forests and villages, tribes and peasants rose again and again because the British (and the moneylenders and planters who came with them) took their land, forests and freedom. These revolts were local and were put down, but several forced the British to pass protective laws afterwards — showing the uprisings were not wholly in vain.

The most exam-worthy ones are below.

| Revolt | Year(s) | Region / community | Leader(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sanyasi Rebellion** | 1770s–1820s | Bengal | ascetics / peasants (seen in *Anandmath*) |
| **Kol Uprising** | 1831–32 | Chotanagpur | Buddho Bhagat |
| **Santhal Hul** | 1855–56 | Rajmahal hills (Bengal-Bihar) | **Sidhu & Kanhu** Murmu |
| **Indigo Revolt** | 1859–60 | Bengal | Digambar & Bishnu Biswas |
| **Munda Ulgulan ('Great Tumult')** | 1899–1900 | Chotanagpur | **Birsa Munda** |
| **Mappila (Moplah) revolts** | 19th c.–1921 | Malabar | Mappila peasants |

Two results worth remembering: after the **Santhal Hul**, the British created a special district, the **Santhal Parganas**, and made it illegal for a Santhal to sell land to a non-Santhal. Natural **indigo** farming died out in the early 20th century because German factories invented cheap **synthetic (aniline) dyes**, making Indian indigo unprofitable.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

Prelims regularly asks "which revolt is called Ulgulan?" or matches tribal leaders to their rebellions. These are easy marks if the special terms and leader-names are fixed in memory.

## Picture it

```
1831-32  Kol        - Buddho Bhagat
1855-56  Santhal Hul- Sidhu & Kanhu   -> Santhal Parganas created
1859-60  Indigo     - Digambar & Bishnu Biswas (Neel Darpan, 1860)
1899-1900 Ulgulan   - Birsa Munda      -> Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908
```

## Terms explained

- **Ulgulan** — a Mundari word meaning "Great Tumult"; it is the name of Birsa Munda's rebellion (1899–1900).
- **Hul** — the Santhal word for their 1855–56 uprising.
- **Diku** — the Munda word for "outsider" (moneylenders, landlords, officials) whom the tribals opposed.
- **Ryot** — a peasant/cultivator (the indigo revolt was a ryots' protest).
- **Aniline / synthetic dye** — a man-made chemical dye that replaced natural indigo.

## Don't confuse

- **Ulgulan = Birsa Munda (Munda, 1899–1900)**; **Hul = Santhal (Sidhu-Kanhu, 1855–56)**. These two are the most-swapped pair.
- The term "First War of Independence" for 1857 came from **V.D. Savarkar**; the British called it a "Sepoy Mutiny" — don't attribute it to a tribal revolt.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Ulgulan — Birsa; Hul — Santhal."** Birsa Munda is honoured on **Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (15 November)**.

## TL;DR

- 'Ulgulan' (Great Tumult) = Birsa Munda's Munda rebellion, 1899–1900 (Chotanagpur); Janjatiya Gaurav Divas = 15 Nov.
- Santhal Hul (1855–56) led by Sidhu & Kanhu; afterwards British created the Santhal Parganas with a land-transfer ban.
- Kol Uprising (1831–32, Chotanagpur); Sanyasi Rebellion (Bengal, late 18th c.).
- Indigo Revolt (1859–60, Bengal); indigo declined by early 20th c. as synthetic dyes made it unprofitable.
- Savarkar termed 1857 the 'First War of Indian Independence'; British called it a Sepoy Mutiny.
keyPoints: 'Ulgulan' (Great Tumult) = Birsa Munda's Munda rebellion, 1899–1900 (Chotanagpur); Janjatiya Gaurav Divas = 15 Nov.
Santhal Hul (1855–56) led by Sidhu & Kanhu; afterwards British created the Santhal Parganas with a land-transfer ban.
Kol Uprising (1831–32, Chotanagpur); Sanyasi Rebellion (Bengal, late 18th c.).
Indigo Revolt (1859–60, Bengal); indigo declined by early 20th c. as synthetic dyes made it unprofitable.
Savarkar termed 1857 the 'First War of Independence'; British called it a Sepoy Mutiny.

items.title: For Mains — The Revolt of 1857
items.body:
## In one line

For Mains (GS Paper-II, M2-4), 1857 is rarely asked as plain facts — it is asked as an argument: what caused it, what was its real nature, why it failed, and how it reshaped British India.

## The story

Mains answers must move from narration to analysis. Use the dimension table below to decide what the question is really testing, then pick 3–4 dimensions and build intro–body–conclusion around them.

| Dimension | What to write | Sharp point to quote |
|---|---|---|
| **Causes** | Five heads (economic, political, administrative, socio-religious, military) + the spark | Annexation of Awadh (1856); greased cartridge |
| **Nature** | Mutiny vs First War of Independence debate | Savarkar (1909) vs R.C. Majumdar's sceptical view |
| **Why it failed** | Limited spread, no unity, British telegraph, loyal princes | Nizam, Scindia, Holkar, Sikh rulers stayed loyal |
| **Significance / impact** | End of Company rule; Crown rule; army re-organised | GoI Act 1858; Queen's Proclamation 1858; Peel Commission |
| **Limitations** | Feudal, backward-looking leadership; no modern programme | Educated middle class largely aloof |
| **Legacy** | Seeded later nationalism; 'divide and rule' hardened | First collective anti-colonial memory |

**Data / reports / judgments to quote:** (1) Government of India Act, 1858; (2) Queen's Proclamation, 1858 (the "Magna Carta" of the princes); (3) Peel Commission on army reorganisation; (4) Indian Councils Act, 1861; (5) Savarkar's *The Indian War of Independence, 1857* (1909); (6) ~150,000 Indian deaths in suppression.

**AP angle:** the Deccan and the Telugu districts (Coastal Andhra and the Ceded Districts/Rayalaseema) stayed largely quiet because the **Nizam of Hyderabad** backed the British; but **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt (1846–47)** in the Kurnool region is cited as an early precursor of armed anti-British resistance in the Telugu country, about a decade before 1857.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

M2-4 explicitly lists "1857" alongside British rule, land revenue and nationalism, so examiners expect you to link 1857 to the wider colonial story, not treat it in isolation.

## Terms explained

- **Historiography** — the study of how different historians have interpreted an event (here, mutiny vs war of independence).
- **Magna Carta of the princes** — a nickname for the Queen's Proclamation of 1858 because it guaranteed princes' rights.

## Don't confuse

- The question "was it a national war?" wants a *balanced verdict* (began as a mutiny, gained popular character), not a one-sided yes/no.

## Use in answers

- **Example to cite:** the proclamation of Bahadur Shah Zafar as a unifying symbol — evidence of its popular, not merely military, character.
- **Quote:** Savarkar's phrase "the First War of Indian Independence" versus the official "Sepoy Mutiny" to frame the debate.
- **Diagram idea:** a before/after arrow — "Company rule → (Revolt 1857) → Crown rule" — to open or close the answer.

## TL;DR

- Treat 1857 as an argument: causes → nature → failure → impact → legacy.
- Anchor with named instruments: GoI Act 1858, Queen's Proclamation 1858, Peel Commission, ICA 1861.
- Use the Savarkar-vs-sceptics debate for the "nature" dimension and give a balanced verdict.
- AP angle: Nizam's loyalty kept the Telugu country quiet; Narasimha Reddy (1846–47) as precursor.
